source_contexts.quote: The original strawberry-cofermented coffee was blended with a traditional washed lot from Sebastián’s farm. That blended lot was then sent to the decaffeination facility, where it underwent a fascinating and confusing science experiment known as Ethyl Acetate Decaffeination (EAD). The TL;DR: a sugar alcohol byproduct is used as a solvent to help dissolve 95-97% of the caffeine out of the coffee as it is steamed. This method removes caffeine while preserving flavor profile - a feat scarcely accomplished by the decaf coffees of our youth.

If you’ve sampled one of Sebastián’s original Red Fruits lots in the past, you may remember it for its funky intensity and BIG red fruit energy. By both blending this co-ferment with a washed lot and sending it through the EAD process, we’ve turned that intensity down a notch and amped up the sweetness. It’s still fruited and fun, like strawberry jam and chocolate cherries – but it’s also smooth and sweet, like dulce de leche and milk chocolate. It’s easily one of the most exciting flavor profiles we’ve ever tasted as a decaf, and we think you’ll be nodding your head in quiet agreement as you take your first sip during that 3 pm slump.

source_contexts.quote: Another reason we love our partners at Equation Coffee is because of their profound commitment to community. Since 2013, they have fostered meaningful relationships with over 100 coffee-growing families in the area surrounding their production facility, partnering with them through relationship-driven programs such as Neighbors & Crops. These programs have changed the lives of many coffee growers in Colombia, and Diego Horta is one such beneficiary. This release was grown by Diego on his farm in Santa Maria and then shipped over to the processing gurus at La Palma y El Tucán. After tasting this coffee, we feel certain you'll agree that their partnership is a perfect match.

TRUST THE PROCESS | After being picked at peak ripeness, the coffee cherries are transported to the La Palma processing facility in Cundinamarca, where they undergo 190 hours of anaerobic fermentation in GrainPro bags. Then, they begin the drying process in mechanical dryers for 24 hours before being removed to a coffee drying shed to finish up, achieving optimal moisture content about eight days later.

TAKE A SIP | The red fruit notes in this cup are pronounced and profound, reminding us of black cherries and almost grape-like in character. It’s boozy-but-also-sweet, like cherry cordial filling, and that sweetness feels smooth and creamy, like marzipan. Citrus notes play well with a cinnamon-like spice, giving us a delightful spiced orange note. As the cup cools, it finishes like craft chocolate—and it smells just like walking into Videri Chocolate Factory.

source_contexts.quote: MEET THE PRODUCER | Franky Stiven Hoyos is a third generation farmer from Huila, and he is one of the many young, multi-generational producers in Colombia who are pushing the boundaries of processing and flavor. Franky’s grandfather began by planting mixed crops on El Encanto, the family farm which Franky now oversees. His father was the first to plant coffee trees on ten of those 45 hectares, and Franky cut his teeth in the industry by learning barista, roasting, and sensory skills. Today, he applies those learned skills in conjunction with his inherited farming wisdom, and Franky has since moved into experimental processing techniques as a result. He farms sustainably and pursues quality relentlessly — and he’s also refreshingly transparent regarding his processing protocols, an attribute which is increasingly sought-after in the specialty coffee landscape of today.

TAKE A SIP | If you’ve been around here for any length of time, you probably already know that we love at least two things: (1) Gesha as a variety, and (2) processing as a frontier. Well, this coffee champions both. It’s expressive and tropical, novel and exciting and so special. If you’re longing for the extension of summer, we implore you to take one sip: you’ll find guava, mango, orange creamsicle, and pink bubblegum. It’s as if every flavor we love about summer found its way to cling to the season in this cup, and we couldn’t love it more.

source_contexts.quote: Swiss Water Process leads to a fantastic decaf coffee that will surprise you with great taste and none of the chemical processing or aftertaste. This ethically sourced blend has multiple origins: Colombia, Ethiopia, Honduras, Mexico and Indonesia. Flavors vary by season and may include sweet graham cracker, citrus, cherry and dark chocolate with a balance of sweetness and acidity and a pleasant mouthfeel.

With regards to acidity and brightness, Kenya is widely recognized as the king of the hill, and our Kenya AB has been selected at auction as an expertly processed, top-notch offering not to be missed. It is cooperatively produced by many small farmers growing in the central Kenyan farmlands surrounding Mt. Kenya. The individual lots are consolidated at the local mill where they undergo a stringent double fermentation method, sometimes referred to as ‘Kenyan Process,’ that accentuates its complexity. The parchment is sun dried on raised beds and transported to the Nairobi Coffee Exchange where it is graded, cupped for quality and ultimately sold at auction.

Kenya has long been established as leader in high-grade East African arabica—its best lots are famed for their fruity, clean, complex profiles, offering balance and pronounced tasting notes of everything from berries and stone fruit to sweet citrus, rightly fetching a handsome auction price. The Nairobi Coffee Exchange auctions are a quality-based payment system that functions as the nerve center of a well-oiled industry built upon decades of lab-based agri-research, applied farming and a strong network of cooperatives. At the exchanges small farmers have a ‘seat at the table’ so to speak, where they can access a wide range of international buyers who have the will and capital to outbid one another in the perennial quest for a perfect cup. Truth be told, Kenya’s growers are owed much of today’s industry praise; for generations they have pushed the envelope and tested the limits of farming and processing capabilities in order to embrace advances in growing science. The main growing regions extend from the 17,000-foot, central peak of Mount Kenya all the way to the outskirts of the capital city of Nairobi to the south. Another portion of arabica farmlands lie on the slopes of Mt. Elgon, against Kenya’s western border with Uganda.
Cupping Notes: Very bright acidity, medium body. Notes of currant, black tea and a hint of blackberry.

source_contexts.quote: Mountain Thunder’s Espresso Roast Kona Coffee is a 100% Kona Coffee that is roasted a little longer and at a higher temperature. This decreases the acidity while adding body, making it the perfect roast level for espresso lovers. It is also ideal for making some of the classic coffee drinks like Lattes, Mochas, Cappuccinos, Macchiatos, Cubanos, and Americanos.
Our Espresso Roast Kona Coffee is a dark roast, which creates a slightly bitter taste profile, with noticeable chocolate overtones. The acidity is low, and it has a smooth aftertaste.

Our Kona Espresso Roast Coffee starts its journey to your cup on the slopes of volcanoes in the Kona Coffee Belt. This area on the leeward side of Hawaii Island, Hawaii, has ideal conditions for growing superb gourmet coffee … high elevations with mineral-rich volcanic soil. The gentle, cool mountain weather blesses this area with ideal amounts of sunshine and rain.

We first remove the outer cherry skin and then dry the beans to a precise moisture content. The dried coffee beans are then stored in our temperature and humidity-controlled warehouse. This aging process helps bring out the unique aroma and flavor of our Kona Espresso Coffee. Each bean is sorted multiple times for color, size, and density. This ensures that our Roast Master has only the best of the best Kona Coffee Beans to roast. Any coffee beans that do not meet Mountain Thunder standards are sold off to wholesalers and never sold under the Mountain Thunder label.

Our Espresso Roast Coffee is packaged in specially-designed multi-layer bags with one-way air valves. Just before sealing the bag, we flush out oxygen using food-grade nitrogen to make sure that your coffee will stay fresh and arrive with that unmistakable aroma of Kona Coffee.

Teddy started Karamo in 2020, after his family’s farm won that year’s inaugural Ethiopian Cup of Excellence with a natural lot called “Karamo.” Farmers contributing to Karamo’s lots grow local heirloom varieties at extraordinary elevations, where production is limited but quality potential is exceptional. This lot from Agena station brings is composed of deliveries from approximately 500 smallholder farmers, with farms situated at elevations of up to 2,500 masl. The resulting cup is clean, crisp, and complex, with focused stone fruit, dense tropical flavors, white florals, juicy acidity, and coating sweetness.

The Cumbres del Poas micro mill is located in Sabanilla, Alajuela, in the Central Valley region of Costa Rica. Both Francisca and Oscar believe in preserving the environment. In 2009, they became pioneers of high-quality honey and natural-process coffees in Central America when they began experimenting with unique processes. Mill water use is minimal since their coffees do not undergo the washed method. During harvest, they measure the brix content in the coffee cherries to determine the best time to pick for the sweetest, most fruit-forward profile.
This coffee is lightly roasted and is sure to please with its chocolate, black cherry, and strawberry notes.

source_contexts.quote: FLAVOR PROFILE (What we taste)

The dominant flavor note of this coffee that we taste is blackberry but think dark berries. Over the years, we have roasted and tasted lots of coffees with blackberry notes but this is the most balanced and most enjoyable one we have ever tasted.

As a light roast, this coffee has floral and blackberry notes, moderate sweetness, lower to moderate acidity, and a heavier body. Using a scale of 0-10, we place the sweetness at a 6, the acidity at a 3, the body at a 7, and no bitterness.

As a medium-dark roast, this coffee has blackberry and caramelized sugar notes, moderate sweetness, lower acidity, and a heavier body. Using a scale of 0-10, we place the sweetness at a 5-7, the acidity at a 2, the body at a 7, and no bitterness.

As a light roast, we have only brewed it as a filter and immersion but will in time experiment with it as espresso. As a lighter roasted coffee, we recommend starting with a water temperature between 201-208F depending on brew method as lighter roasts are more prone to under extraction. If the coffee tastes sour, 1) grind finer, 2) gradually increase the water temperature, and/or decrease the amount of ground coffee or water used to increase the extraction. If the coffee tastes bitter and over extracted, 1) coarsen up the grind size, 2) gradually decrease the water temperature, and/or 3) increase the amount of ground coffee or decrease the amount of water used. For filter/drip and immersion, we recommend starting with a brewing ratio of 1:15 (e.g., 20 grams of coffee to 300 grams of water), but this again is an area you will adjust for taste preferences. Common ratios are 1:15 to 1:17. If you decide to brew it as espresso, we would recommend using a higher water temperature (e.g., 203-205F) if your machine allows and starting with a 1:3 ratio (e.g., 18 grams of coffee to 54 grams of coffee in the cup), but experimenting with longer and shorter ratios until you find the balance of flavors you prefer.

As a medium-dark roast, this coffee is versatile and is great brewed as filter/drip, immersion, cold brew, and espresso. We recommend starting with a water temperature of 198-201F depending on the brew method as darker roasts are more prone to over extraction. source_contexts.quote: Catuai makes up a majority of the coffee cultivated at Finca San Jeronimo in Guatemala, located on the side of Volcan Atitlan, and is a consistently approachable and slightly bright coffee. The washed process allowing us to taste the terroir, without additional fermentation time coming into play. We paired the catuai with a washed coffee from the Pacas Family's mill, Cafe Tuxpal, in El Salvador. Together, the sweet, nutty profile of these Salvadoran beans pairs well with the brighter, baking spice notes from the Catuai.
